title: Know who you work for (Avot 2:14)
hookLine: be eager to learn, and know before whom you labor

lines: THE QUESTION AT THE DINNER TABLE.
cards: A kid at the dinner table, usually when a guest is there, asks the big one. How do you know God is real? Or, why do we even do this?
The adults glance at each other, and somebody says, eat your peas.
Today's sage, the last of the five students, is Rabbi Elazar, usually identified as Elazar ben Arach: the student whose answer won, the one with the good heart.
His saying starts by telling you to be ready for that question.

teach.b: Rabbi Elazar says: be eager to learn Torah. Know what to answer an apikoros. And know before whom you toil, and that your employer can be trusted to pay you the wage of your work.

Apikoros echoes the name Epicurus, a Greek philosopher who taught that the gods take no interest in human affairs. In rabbinic Hebrew, an apikoros is a scoffer, someone who mocks the faith and its teachers.
Rabbi Elazar doesn't say avoid them, or shout them down. He says study well enough to answer. Don't be caught with only eat your peas.
There's a quieter reading too: sometimes the skeptic is the voice in your own head at two in the morning, and knowing what to answer means learning enough to face your own questions honestly.

Then the second half: know before whom you toil. All your learning and work happen in front of someone. A related line in the Talmud, sometimes written above the ark in synagogues, says know before whom you stand.
Then a picture from the workplace: your employer is trustworthy, and will pay your wages. The employer, in this saying, is God.

In the saying's picture, the work put into learning and living well isn't lost, even when no one else seems to notice. Learn hard, be ready for hard questions, and remember who you're really working for.

how: Jewish learning makes room for hard questions, and the words 'know before whom you stand' appear above the ark in some synagogues as a reminder during prayer.

o: a sincere seeker with honest questions about God
a scribe who copies Torah scrolls by hand
a scoffer who mocks the faith and its teachers

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: a scoffer, a mocker of the faith
your work is done before God

s: the saying begins with eagerness to learn
be eager to learn Torah is its first line.
Rabbi Elazar says to avoid anyone who asks hard questions
he says know what to answer them. study well enough to reply.
the employer in the saying is your boss at work
it's God, who will pay the wage of your learning and living well.

games.q: at dinner, a guest's teenager asks, how do you even know any of this is true? what does Rabbi Elazar's saying suggest?
o: answer honestly, from what you've learned.
tell them it's rude to ask.
games.why: know what to answer an apikoros, he says: study well enough to face hard questions honestly.

practice: Let one hard question come up, about faith, or meaning, or why people do what they do, your own or one a child or friend has asked you. Don't rush to answer it; just hold it honestly.
Then ask what one thing you could learn, a book, a person to ask, a page of text, that would help you answer it better.

wordCard.voice: Apikoros. A scoffer, a skeptic of the faith: the one Rabbi Elazar says to study hard enough to answer, while remembering before whom you toil.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: know before whom you toil.

carryVoice: Your line: know before whom you toil. A hard question deserves a real answer. That's day two hundred sixty-two.
